title: How the Power Grid Keeps Your Lights On, Every Second
summary: Follow one spark from the generator to your bulb, then meet the people who keep supply and demand balanced at 60 Hz. Plus the ordinary cause behind North America's worst blackout.
sources: Supply must match demand for the grid to stay stable; transformers step voltage up and down between the power plant, long-distance lines and distribution lines; the Eastern and Western interconnections are linked to Canada's grid (EIA, Electricity explained: delivery to consumers): https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/delivery-to-consumers.php

Nearly 160,000 miles of high-voltage power lines; a balancing authority ensures, in real time, that power system demand and supply are finely balanced (EIA, Today in Energy, 20 Jul 2016): https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=27152

The lower 48 run on interconnections (Eastern, Western, Texas/ERCOT) that operate at a synchronized frequency averaging 60 Hz (US DOE Office of Electricity, Learn more about interconnections): https://www.energy.gov/oe/learn-more-about-interconnections

US utility-scale generation in 2025: renewables about 24%; natural gas about 41%, nuclear about 18%, coal about 17%, wind about 11%, solar about 7%, hydropower about 6% (EIA, Electricity explained: electricity in the US): https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/electricity/electricity-in-the-us.php

Transmission and distribution losses averaged about 5% of the electricity transmitted and distributed in the US in 2018 through 2022 (EIA FAQ, updated 7 Nov 2023): https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=105&t=3
ERCOT serves more than 27 million Texas customers, about 90 percent of the state's electric load (ERCOT, About ERCOT): https://www.ercot.com/about

More than half of the electricity in Canada (60%) is generated from hydroelectricity; 625.7 TWh produced in 2021 (Canada Energy Regulator, Canada Energy Profile): https://cer-rec.gc.ca/en/data-analysis/energy-markets/provincial-territorial-energy-profiles/provincial-territorial-energy-profiles-canada.html

August 14, 2003, saw the worst blackout in North American history; the causes the US-Canada task force named include inadequate situational awareness and inadequate tree trimming (US DOE, Blackout 2003: task force final report, 5 Apr 2004): https://www.energy.gov/oe/articles/blackout-2003-us-canada-task-force-presents-final-report-onblackout-august-2003

scenes.narration: Right now, power plants are making just as much electricity as everyone is using. Not more. Not less.
That's the rule. For the grid to stay stable, supply has to match demand.
So how does the grid pull that off, every second of every day?
When it slips, the lights go out. In {2003|two thousand three}, North America had its worst blackout ever. And one cause was growing right outside.
By the end, you'll know how one spark gets from a power plant to your wall, who keeps the balance, and what that cause was.
Part one: the trip.
Follow one spark. It starts at a generator.
Last year, about {41%|forty-one percent} of America's power came from natural gas.
Then nuclear, about {18%|eighteen}, and coal, about {17%|seventeen}. Wind, solar and hydro made most of the rest.
A transformer cranks the voltage way up for the long trip.
High voltage carries power long distances more efficiently. The US has nearly {160,000|a hundred and sixty thousand} miles of these lines.
Even so, some power gets lost on the way: about {5%|five percent} in transmission and distribution.
Near town, a substation steps the voltage back down.
The can on your pole steps it down again, and the spark reaches your bulb.
If you like seeing how things really work, subscribe. There's a new system every Sunday.
Part two: the balance.
Here's the hard part. Nobody calls the grid before switching on an oven. It just has to keep up.
Across each grid, the power runs at one shared beat: about {60|sixty} cycles a second.

data.source: US DOE · GRID FREQUENCY AVERAGES 60 HZ

scenes.narration: Keeping that balance is the job of balancing authorities. In real time, they keep supply and demand finely balanced.
And there isn't one big US grid. The lower {48|forty-eight} mostly run on three: the East, the West, and Texas.
Texas mostly runs its own. ERCOT serves about {90%|ninety percent} of the state's electric load: more than {27 million|twenty-seven million} customers.
North of the border, Canada leans on water. About {60%|sixty percent} of its electricity comes from hydro. And the East and West grids link up with Canada's.
Part three: the cause.
Back to {2003|two thousand three}. The task force that studied the blackout named its causes. Blind spots in the control rooms were on the list.
So was something much more ordinary: trees. Inadequate tree trimming.
That's the grid: a spark stepped up, sent out and stepped down, while people balance supply and demand every second. And somebody trims the trees.
Pick a pipe for the next system. New one every Sunday.
